paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Part 1. You will hear a man calling a sports centre to ask about a swimming course. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 7.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre, Emma speaking. How can I help you?

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: Hi, I'm calling about your swimming courses for adults. I saw a poster and I'd like some more information.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Of course. I'll just take a few details first. Can I have your name, please?

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: Yes, it's Daniel Fairbank. That's F, A, I, R, B, A, N, K.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Thank you, Daniel. And what is your address?

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: It's 14 Kestrel Road. Kestrel is spelt K, E, S, T, R, E, L.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Lovely. Now, we run two adult courses. There's a beginner course for people who can't swim at all, and an improver course for people who can already swim a little but want to get better.

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: I can manage a couple of lengths, but my technique is terrible, so I think the improver course is the one for me.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Okay. The improver course runs on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, but I'm afraid Tuesday is already full.

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: That's fine, Thursday suits me better anyway.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Great. The course lasts eight weeks, with one session a week.

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: Eight weeks. Okay.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: And is there anything in particular you want to work on? It helps the instructor plan the sessions.

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: Mainly my breathing. I get out of breath really quickly. And I'd like to build up my stamina so I can swim for longer.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Breathing and stamina. I'll note that down. And can I ask how you heard about the course? Was it our website?

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: No, actually, a colleague at work told me about it. She did the course last year.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: That's nice to hear.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Now listen and answer questions 8 to 10.

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: Do I need to be a member of the centre to join the course?

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Yes, you do. There are three types of membership. Standard membership is thirty-two pounds a month and covers both the gym and the pool.

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: And the others?

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: Off-peak membership is twenty-four pounds a month. It's the same facilities, but you can only use them before four p.m. on weekdays.

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: Hmm, the course is in the evening, so that won't work for me.

paragraphs.label: Receptionist
paragraphs.text: No, probably not. Then there's family membership at fifty-eight pounds, which includes free parking for children's activities. Some families find that very useful.

paragraphs.label: Daniel
paragraphs.text: I don't have children, so I'll go for standard. Thanks very much.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have some time to check your answers.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at a wetland park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hollowmere Wetland Park. We're standing outside the visitor centre, at the southern end of the park, and you should all have a copy of the map. Let me point out a few places before you set off.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: As you leave the visitor centre and face the lake, the cafe is immediately on your left, on the western side. It opens at nine, so it's a good place to start the day.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: If you're interested in birds, head for the bird hide. It's at the north-western corner of the lake, where the reeds are thickest. It's a long walk, but the views are worth it.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: On the way there you'll pass the boardwalk. It runs out over the water from the west shore of the lake, about halfway up. Please take care, because it can be slippery after rain.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: Families with young children will want the play area. It's just on your right as you leave this building, so on the eastern side, opposite the cafe.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: Finally, the picnic area is right up at the far end of the park, next to the North Gate, just to the east of it. There are tables there, and some shelter if it rains.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: A little history. Many visitors assume this land was always farmland, and it's true that there were farms nearby. But the park itself was created on an old quarry. When the quarry closed, the deep pits filled with water and became the lake you see today.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: A few rules. Dogs are welcome as long as they're kept on a lead. You're welcome to feed the ducks, but please use the special food sold in the cafe. And we ask you not to ride bicycles on the boardwalk, because it's too narrow to pass safely.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: We also run a guided bat walk. People often think it's only in summer, but in fact it runs all year, on the first Saturday of each month, starting at dusk.

paragraphs.label: Guide
paragraphs.text: And before you go: there are a few things you can borrow free of charge from the visitor centre. We lend binoculars, and we also have wheelchairs available for anyone who needs one. We don't lend fishing equipment, I'm afraid, as fishing isn't allowed here, and we used to lend umbrellas, but too many of them never came back!

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have some time to check your answers.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Kate and Josh, discussing their research project with their tutor, Dr Hale. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: Come in, both of you. So, how is the project on noise in student housing going?

paragraphs.label: Kate
paragraphs.text: Quite well, thanks. You might remember you originally suggested we look at energy use in the halls, but we went with noise in the end.

paragraphs.label: Josh
paragraphs.text: Yes, that was really because of my own flat. It was so noisy last year that I could hardly sleep, so we were both curious about how common the problem was.

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: And how did you collect your data?

paragraphs.label: Kate
paragraphs.text: We started with a questionnaire, but hardly anyone returned it. So most of our data came from sound meters that we left in kitchens and corridors in three different halls.

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: Did that go smoothly?

paragraphs.label: Josh
paragraphs.text: Mostly. The batteries lasted fine, but a few times students moved the meters, so we lost a couple of nights of readings from one of the kitchens.

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: That happens. Now, I've read your draft literature review. The length is fine, but most of the studies you cite are over fifteen years old. I'd like you to include some more recent research.

paragraphs.label: Kate
paragraphs.text: Okay, we can do that.

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: And what surprised you most in the results?

paragraphs.label: Josh
paragraphs.text: For me, it was that the kitchens were much noisier than the corridors. We expected the opposite, because the corridors are where people come in late at night. Kate was more surprised that the weekends weren't much worse than weekdays.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: Let's go through the report section by section. The introduction is clear and well organised. I wouldn't change it.

paragraphs.label: Kate
paragraphs.text: Great. What about the method section?

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: It's accurate, but it's hard to picture where the meters were. A diagram showing their positions in each hall would help a lot.

paragraphs.label: Josh
paragraphs.text: We can draw that. And the raw data tables? They take up nearly ten pages.

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: They're useful, but they interrupt the reading. Move them to an appendix and just keep the summary chart in the main text.

paragraphs.label: Kate
paragraphs.text: And the discussion?

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: That needs the most work. At the moment it repeats the results instead of explaining them, so I'd like you to rewrite it completely.

paragraphs.label: Josh
paragraphs.text: Okay. And the section with our personal reflections?

paragraphs.label: Dr Hale
paragraphs.text: Honestly, it doesn't belong in a research report. I'd cut it altogether.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have some time to check your answers.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about mangrove forests. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Good afternoon. Today I'm going to talk about mangrove forests, which are among the most productive and also the most threatened ecosystems on Earth.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Mangroves are trees that grow along tropical coastlines, in the intertidal zone, that is, the area between land and sea that is covered by water at high tide and exposed at low tide.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Living in seawater is difficult for a tree. Many mangrove species deal with this through their roots, which filter out most of the salt before the water is drawn up into the plant.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: The mud they grow in also contains very little air. To cope with this, some species produce special roots that grow upwards, out of the mud, so that they can take in oxygen directly from the atmosphere.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Why do mangroves matter? First, they protect coastlines. The dense network of roots reduces the energy of waves, which means less erosion and less damage during storms.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Second, mangroves are extremely good at storing carbon. Most of it is not in the trees themselves but in the soil beneath them, where it can remain for thousands of years.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Third, the sheltered water between the roots acts as a nursery for young fish, many of which later move out to coral reefs or the open sea.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Unfortunately, mangroves are disappearing. The biggest single cause in recent decades has been clearing land for shrimp farms. Another serious problem is plastic. Floating plastic waste collects among the roots and smothers the seedlings, so new trees cannot establish themselves.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Many countries have tried to restore lost mangroves by planting, but the results have often been disappointing. In a number of projects, the young trees were placed too low on the shore, where they were underwater for too long each day, and most of them died.

paragraphs.label: Lecturer
paragraphs.text: Researchers now agree that the best results come not from planting at all, but from restoring the natural water flow, for example by removing old walls and channels. When the water moves freely again, mangroves usually return on their own.

paragraphs.label: Narrator
paragraphs.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have some time to check your answers. That is the end of the listening test.
